Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is the fastest way to earn money?
Old_Answer: Last weekend, I made $5000 in a little more than 20 minutes. Here’s a picture to prove it. No, I didn’t sell drugs. I didn’t become a pornstar. I didn’t even start a business. I competed in a martial arts tournament, and I won. That’s it. I had 3 matches. The first match lasted 8 minutes. The second match went for about 2 minutes, and the 3rd and final match went for 10 minutes. I was on the mat fighting for a little more than 20 minutes. I won all 3 matches, and I was awarded a $5000 prize for my efforts. $5000 in 20 minutes of work. An easy day at the office, right? Wrong. Very wrong. There wasn’t much about this weekend that was easy, but, it was very quick. I endured quite a bit of pain, for a moderate amount of time, and I was awarded money — only because I was successful. I did make $5000 in 20 minutes, but in reality, it took me about 12 years to develop the skills to even have a chance at winning this tournament on Saturday. I made $5000 in 20 minutes, but in the long run, when it comes to my Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu “career” (a word I didn’t feel comfortable even using until about 6 months ago), I’ve lost a lot of money over the last 7 years. That’s why I wanted to write this answer about long-term goals and short-term payoffs. It takes a ridiculous amount of time to do something at a high level. I am not the most talented athlete. I’m not the most talented at anything. I don’t have magic genetics that made me a high-level athlete from a young age. When I played baseball growing up, it took me 2 years to develop enough hand-eye coordination just to hit the fucking ball. I spent the first 2 years of my baseball career celebrating foul balls and “foul tips” because they were “contact”. Contact was my indication of progress. I tried out for my school’s basketball team in middle school when I realized that the baseball thing wasn’t really working out, and I didn’t get past the first cut in basketball. Unfortunately, being 4'11 and chubby doesn’t exactly help you get the coach’s attention at basketball tryouts. After that was when I started wrestling, and I didn’t exactly have any success on the wrestling mat at first either. In 8th grade (my second year of wrestling — you know, when I was supposed to be better than my first year), I finished with 4 wins and 28 losses (more than double the amount of losses of my first year). Most of the losses were from pins. I spent most of my first 2 years involved in combat sports getting thrown around the ring, getting pinned, and then crying in the bleachers while munching on the post-competition Snickers bar that my mom or dad bought me. The point is, I wasn’t a talented wrestler, either. By my senior year of high school, I was winning more matches than I was losing, but I wasn’t winning tournaments. I never qualified for the state tournament. I wasn’t good, and I got better, but I never became great. Once wrestling was done, I started Jiu-Jitsu. This was the first time I was able to excel at something, but my success has never been linear. It takes a ridiculously strong mind to do something at a high level. When I started Jiu-Jitsu, I didn’t have any success either. I came in with a wrestling background, and that meant that I was supposed to have instant success in Jiu-Jitsu, but I didn’t. Again, I was winning more than I was losing, but I wasn’t great at Jiu-Jitsu and I didn’t have great results in Jiu-Jitsu. I was solid, but solid does not mean great. My goal wasn’t to be “solid”. My goal was to be world-class. Finally, at around 19, I started to get my “man-body”. That helped. But muscles alone weren’t enough to help me achieve my goals. I also had to develop world-class technique, precise timing, and a mind that could do all these things under intense pressure. What shifted over the course of that ridiculously long amount of time that I spent competing in martial arts was that I developed the mind of a successful martial arts competitor. I did this by studying philosophy, writing about my anxiety, practicing good habits, and yes, training a metric fuck-ton of Jiu-Jitsu on top of that. Now that I’m doing fairly well in Jiu-Jitsu, a lot of people seem to assume that I’m this talented guy who has some abilities that other people don’t have or that I just have ridiculously good luck. Those people weren’t here 11 years ago when I looked like a “roly-poly” on the mat — my dad’s words. I’ve done what I do with an intense amount of focus for a very long time. That’s pretty much it. That’s more important than talent. That’s more important than hard work. That’s more important than anything if you ask me. It takes a village to do something at a high level. Okay, this answer has been all about me so far. It’s time to shift the focus. For a long time, I was really concerned with being “self-made”. I wanted everyone to know that I had worked my ass off for everything that I achieve. I wanted everyone to know that I did it all myself. The problem is, that wouldn’t be the truth. I didn’t do this all on my own. I had a lot of help. In the picture above, the guy on my left (Jack) has been traveling with me and competing with me for nearly the last 4 years, and the guy on my right (my coach, Jeff) has been teaching me most of the Jiu-Jitsu I know since I was 17-years-old. Those are just 2 of the people that make up this village of friends and teammates that I have that help me do the things that I do at a high level. I’m just a vessel or something. Apart from just my training partners at the gym, there are also the guys who I’ve met through training out of town who have pushed me to reach for goals that I previously couldn’t have fathomed, and there are also the countless strangers who have said nice (and not-so-nice) things to me on the internet for the last year and a half that I’ve been sharing my life through writing. Both the good and bad comments motivate me in different ways. If you clicked on this answer because you wanted to learn about how to make $5000 in 20 minutes, I apologize immediately. I can’t teach you fast and easy ways to succeed. I can, however, show you that quick success does not exist. None of the things that I do well come easy to me. I could never win any grappling tournaments without training and working my butt off. I could never write good writing without editing it an obnoxious amount of times. I could never make good decisions without making stupid ones first. Maybe you’re the same way. Maybe my “advice” is useless, and maybe you’re going to go into your life and do the opposite of what I say. If that’s you, I respect it. I’ve been that guy. However, those readers are not the reason I write. I write for the people who can and are willing to learn for me. First and foremost, the person who can learn the most from the dumb shit I’ve done is myself. Here’s to not making the same mistakes over and over again.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is the best way to make money?
Old_Answer: Making money is harder when it comes from something you love. I’ve been doing Jiu-Jitsu for about 7 years, competing for more than 6 years, and competing at the “world level” for about 5 years. I didn’t start making enough money to live as an athlete until this year—2022. Originally, I thought that money didn’t exist in Jiu-Jitsu. Jiu-Jitsu, as I understood it, was an amateur sport. Then, I realized something. I didn’t realize it on my own, either. I realized it because of a friend who was a few steps above me in his career. He had a much more professional approach than I did. Jiu-Jitsu was an amateur sport for me because I was competing in amateur events. I wasn’t getting paid because I was taking every opportunity to compete possible. I didn’t really care if there was money on the line, a gold medal, or just some social clout. I loved Jiu-Jitsu, so I just fought because I loved it. I wasn’t a professional though. Looking back, this approach had some great benefits (I got a lot of experience, became good at competing, and became good at handling competition nerves), but it also had some drawbacks too. I got injured a lot, didn’t make money most of the time, and I spent a lot of my own money and time traveling to events, training myself, and working weird jobs to pay for competitions and travel. What a lot of people don’t realize is that most of the medal pictures I post on here won me zero dollars. I used medals as a way of building my teaching pedigree, but I didn’t get paid directly from competition until earlier this year. The only thing that changed was my mindset. I stopped viewing myself as “a grinder” and started viewing myself as a racehorse. I started viewing myself as a prizefighter. If that sounds pretentious to you, don’t worry. I didn’t like it at first either. In sports, it’s not smarter to fight every weekend. UFC fighters fight 3–4 times per year, and that’s a very active year. Jiu-Jitsu is less taxing than MMA, so I figured I could compete every couple of weeks without a problem. I had a meeting with a strength coach, and when I told him about my competition schedule, he basically laughed at me for thinking it was possible to be at my best every weekend without consequences. He told me about a bodybuilder who was hustling like a lunatic, trying to maintain peak performance every weekend, and using small shows (where he was paid $500 or less) to make his living. After about 6 months, he died. So what’s the point? The point is that you can’t nickel and dime your way to big success. You need to take stepping stones, but if you never take big shots, you’ll never get the big wins. I ain’t rich, but I’m also not fighting for free anymore. I make several times what I did last year and I’m doing the same things. The best way to make money is to know your worth and not accept anything less that what you are worth. If you can do this, you will get ahead of most people. Oh, but there’s a caveat. If you think you’re worth $1000 per hour, you better work like someone who’s worth $1000 an hour. You better deliver at least $1000 per hour worth of benefit to your customers. Skill pays. If you want to make money, do whatever it is you do really fucking well.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Is martial arts a lifestyle?
Old_Answer: I could have had a very normal life. My parents live relatively “normal lives”. My non martial arts friends live pretty normal lives. I had a mostly normal childhood (although, probably a bit more exposure to mental illness than the average person). Doing the normal stuff—getting a regular job, going to normal social gatherings with friends, or other normal people things (like going to the movies or the mall or whatever)—was definitely an option for me. That was going to be, until the first day I walked into a Jiu-Jitsu academy. I know it sometimes sounds like that I’m bragging when I say that I “gave up a normal life for this”, but that’s not my intention. Really, I’m just trying to understand the bizarre reality that I’ve created myself. I literally fight crazy people for money. This is my job right now. Sorry if I think it’s weird. The other thing that I think that is really important to understand that the average martial artist doesn’t go through their life the same way I do. For me, martial arts is a lifestyle because it’s literally my entire life. Jiu-Jitsu is my favorite sport, my passion, and my job. For other people, martial arts is their hobby. This means that it might be part of their lifestyle, but that doesn’t mean that their whole lifestyle is martial arts-related. The beauty of martial arts is that you get out what you put in. If you want new friends, personal development, or maybe even a job, you can get that from martial arts by investing hours upon hours of your time. If you just want to get in better shape, you get that too. It’s up to you.
Answer_with_writing_sample: Absolutely, martial arts is much more than just a sport or a hobby; it’s a lifestyle that seeps into every aspect of your daily routine and mindset. When I first stepped onto the mat, I thought I was just signing up for self-defense and fitness. Little did I know that it would become a core part of my identity. Training becomes a part of your schedule, your discipline, and your commitments. It’s not just about the physical practice; it shapes your mental resilience, your approach to challenges, and how you view the world. Every time I step into the gym, it’s a reminder that I’m part of a community that values respect, perseverance, and growth. You learn to embrace discomfort, whether it’s getting tapped out in sparring or waking up early for that extra session. And it doesn’t stop at the gym; principles like humility and respect guide your interactions outside of martial arts. The struggles you face on the mat—like overcoming fear, pushing through fatigue, and handling failure—translate beautifully into life’s battles. You start to see challenges in work or relationships through the lens of a martial artist, processing setbacks as opportunities for growth. Honestly, when I think about it, my journey in martial arts has been as transformative as any life lesson I’ve learned. It’s more than just technique or belts; it’s about cultivating a mindset that prioritizes continuous self-improvement and a sense of community, making it an irreplaceable lifestyle.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Why do people write such lengthy answers on Quora?
Old_Answer: I started writing on Quora because in July of 2021, I read Nicolas Cole’s book, The Art and Business of Online Writing. (This is not an ad for that book btw. I don’t know Mr. Cole and apart from the $9.80 I spent on buying his book, I never have given him any of my money. The book was just a great way to learn about different places to write on the internet) That book was literally the whole reason I revisited Quora after years of barely scrolling through the site. I had created a Quora account years before, but I was too anxious to publish anything and I naively thought that writing on Quora “wouldn’t be worth it”. The reason that I decided to write on Quora in the first place was because I thought it would help me get better at writing while putting myself in front of a new audience (I started writing on Medium 10 months before I posted my first Quora answer). So yes. I started writing on Quora beacuse I wanted to advance my career. That was basically the only reason. I didn’t start writing on Quora because I’m some saint who just wants to help people. I didn’t start writing on Quora because I thought it would make me money. I started writing on Quora because I thought it would help me improve my skills to the point where I could maybe make money in the future. And? I was sort of right, but it took a while. Along the way, I’ve come to love Quora for what it really is: the Wild West of Digital Writing. Quora is not a traditional “Question and Answer” site. This isn’t a site for learning basic information. It’s not a site where you’re going to learn who the 23rd president of the United States was (although, for the sake of contradicting myself, it was Benjamin Harrison). This is a storytelling website. My first 89 Quora answers got around 6000 views cumulative (and not even 30 upvotes), and my 90th answer had several hundred thousand views and nearly 1000 upvotes in just a few days. I didn’t know much about Quora at the time, and I didn’t know much about the value that you could have on a community from a single answer, but my first “viral” answer taught me a lot about what Quora is all about. I’ve gone viral on Quora a bunch of times. One of my answers has more than 2 million views. I’ve realized however, that Quora isn’t about “going viral”. It’s not about answering questions, and it’s not even about “providing value”. The point of Quora goes deeper than whatever it is you have to say. The premise of Quora isn’t “this is what I know”. The premise of Quora is “this is what happened to me, and here’s what I learned”. Each frequently visited question has dozens (oftentimes more) replies and answers, and if you read through all of these answers, you’ll read the perspectives and stories of dozens of different individuals. Individuals. People. You’ll get a bunch of different worldviews, just from clicking on one question. If you click on “How can I overcome the fear of failure?”, you’ll see my essay on middle school wrestling. You’ll see James Altucher’s story of when he quit his job. You’ll some lady’s story of how she became a doctor. You’ll see a lot of really cool stories. The reason that people write long answers here on Quora is not to be pretentious, it’s because they’ve got stories to tell. That’s it, and that’s what I love about Quora. There are barely any rules here, barely any regular people, and a lot of people with freaking awesome stories. It’s the Wild West of Digital Writing., and I think that’s badass.
Answer_with_writing_sample: People write lengthy answers on Quora for a variety of reasons, and the motivations can be as multifaceted as the subjects being discussed. For starters, many writers are deeply passionate about their topics, and they want to share their knowledge and insights in a way that does justice to the subject matter. It’s not just about providing a quick answer; it’s about painting a complete picture. They often feel that a short response would lack depth and nuance, which can be crucial for understanding complex issues. Additionally, lengthy answers allow for storytelling—an effective way to engage readers. By sharing personal experiences or anecdotes, writers can create a connection with their audience, making the information more relatable and impactful. There's also the aspect of credibility; a detailed response can demonstrate expertise and thoroughness, which can enhance the writer’s reputation within the community. They might believe that the more they write, the more they can help others, contributing to a richer discourse. And honestly, there's an element of self-expression involved; for many, writing is a way to process their thoughts and articulate their views. It’s a chance to explore their ideas fully, rather than just scratching the surface. In essence, lengthy answers on Quora reflect a blend of passion, a desire for connection, and a commitment to thoroughness, allowing writers to share not just facts, but deeper insights that resonate with the readers.
Answer_with_user_profile: People often write lengthy answers on Quora for several reasons, and understanding these motivations can provide insight into the platform's dynamics. Firstly, Quora serves as a knowledge-sharing community, and many contributors feel compelled to provide comprehensive and well-rounded responses. This desire to impart knowledge is often rooted in a background in education or professional experience, where individuals have cultivated expertise in specific areas. Moreover, longer answers allow for a nuanced exploration of complex topics, enabling writers to present multiple perspectives and detail their reasoning. Additionally, the Quora algorithm tends to favor detailed answers, as they often receive higher engagement rates and thus can lead to increased visibility for the writer. On a more personal level, for many, writing long answers is a form of intellectual exercise and self-expression, allowing them to articulate their thoughts and opinions in a structured manner. Lastly, the social aspect of Quora plays a significant role; longer, insightful answers can foster discussions and connections with like-minded individuals, creating a sense of community. Ultimately, the blend of knowledge-sharing, credibility-building, engagement strategy, personal expression, and community interaction drives the tendency for users to craft longer responses on Quora.
Answer_with_full_information: People write lengthy answers on Quora for a bunch of reasons, and it often boils down to a mix of personal expression and the desire to genuinely help others. When I see a question that sparks my interest, I often have a lot to say because there’s so much nuance in life's experiences. Lengthy answers allow me to explore those nuances. It’s like peeling back the layers of an onion; the surface may be simple, but the more you dig in, the more complex and rich the insights become. Additionally, I think there’s a natural tendency to want to establish authority or credibility. By providing detailed responses, writers can showcase their expertise or unique perspective based on lived experiences. It can also be therapeutic, allowing the writer to process their thoughts and feelings while crafting a narrative that might resonate with readers. For some, it’s about leaving a legacy of knowledge—like a digital footprint that could help someone down the line. Plus, let's be real, the internet often rewards lengthy and in-depth content with more visibility. So, when writers see that longer posts lead to more engagement, they might feel motivated to keep that length in their writing. Ultimately, it’s a blend of passion, a desire for connection, and the hope that their words will make a meaningful impact in someone else's life. In a world full of quick tweets and fleeting posts, sometimes people just want to take a moment to share their thoughts fully and authentically.

Question: Who are you beyond Quora?
Old_Answer: Here's me, beyond Quora. When I'm not writing, I'm probably either doing Jiu-Jitsu, eating, or sleeping. I train Jiu-Jitsu 2-3 times per day, 6-7 days per week. As I've gotten older and more banged up (this sport isn't exactly great for the ole body), I've begun to vary the intensity of these training sessions, but I'm still in the gym every day multiple times per day. I also teach private lessons and seminars all over the place. That's me off Quora in a nutshell. On Quora, I feel like I'm the "martial arts self-help/life lessons dude", but that's not always who I am in real life. In real life, I'm a 24-year-old (almost 25!) Question: How do I forget someone whom I once loved deeply?
Old_Answer: This question reminds me of my ex-girlfriend who I thought was the love of my life. She told me I was the love of her life, and I believed her. And yet, here we are. Sometimes, I wish I could forget her. If there's anything I learned from the movie in the picture above (Eternal Sunshine of a Spotless Mind), it’s that you're not supposed to forget the people you once loved, even if it hurts to not forget them. You’re supposed to learn from them. This sounds nice in a self-help-esque Quora answer, but it’s really hard to do in reality. My ex who I broke up with last year was the first woman who I really loved. It was the first time I really loved a person who isn’t my mom, my dad, or my sister. I know I really loved her because still, after everything we went through, I can’t hate her or even be mad at her. I know I loved her because I kept trying to convince myself that I wasn’t in love. This love was a neurochemical hijacking in a way I had never experienced before, and though the breakup was more than a year ago now, I still miss her a lot. I’ve dated other people since her, but I still miss her. “There are plenty of fish in the sea”, but I miss her. I would take her back right now, even though doing it would be a horrible decision. Even though taking her back would destroy my mental health, drain the life out of me, and break me down, I know that if she showed up at my doorstep I couldn’t resist her. I think that’s love. I’m only 24 and I don’t know that much, but I don’t think love is always rational. I loved this girl so damn much, and I’ll probably never see her again. I probably shouldn't ever see her again. She was sweet and sensitive, yet strong and determined. She had the duality and complexity that I’ve always craved in a partner, and I miss that so much. But she also had this dark side that terrified me. She changed a lot in the time we were together, and eventually, we grew apart. We grew apart, but that doesn’t mean I lost the memories. For a long time, I wanted the “spotless mind”, just like in the movie. I still remember when she held me one December afternoon in Milwaukee and made me feel like I didn’t have to fight my way through every moment of my life anymore. I still remember when we would sit together on Saturday afternoons after Jiu-Jitsu training and read together. I still remember when we went on drives and talked about Nietzsche, Buddha, and Viktor Frankl. I still miss that stuff, but it’s gone now. Anyway—sorry for my sob story. The point I’m trying to make is that sometimes I wish I could just rip these memories out of my head so that I didn’t have to miss this girl who probably doesn’t even think about me anymore. That’s probably the part that hurts the most. I’m sure she’s moved on. I moved on too, but sometimes it doesn’t feel that way. This past breakup forced me to change the way that I approach moving on. In the past, I’d breakup with someone and drown myself in work and training to forget them, just long enough until I stumbled upon the next girl who I could go through the same toxic cycles with. This past breakup cut me so deep that I had to actually grow. I couldn’t lie anymore. I had to forgive her for hurting me. I had to forgive myself for not being good enough and not knowing enough. I had to forgive all parties involved, but I never forgot any of what happened. The ending hurt so bad that I had no choice but to carefully analyze each mistake each of made so that I could ensure that it wouldn’t happen again. I couldn't sleep for weeks after it happened, so I had all kinds of time. This past breakup changed the way that I view every single person I interact with. It made me more careful, more mature (I think), and more protective of my own peace and wellbeing. I won’t throw myself at anyone without a bloody care ever again. I don’t want to forget these valuable lessons. I don’t want this girl’s memory to haunt me forever, but I don’t want to forget the moments that made me feel so happy and in love. After the breakup, I found myself desperately chasing women in an effort to replace the feelings that I had when I was in love, but no one could satiate my rabid insecure child the way she did. This empty feeling meant to me at the time that I needed to get her back, so I tried to do that. Long story short, it didn’t work. In time (time is the best breakup medicine), I realized that with practice, I could love myself the way my first love loved me. I realized that I wasn’t even really looking for a girlfriend or a partner, I was looking for validation and protection. It didn’t even take a therapist for me to figure why that was something I felt was lacking. With practice, writing, mindfulness, and most importantly genuine self-sufficiency (which I didn’t have during my last relationship), I was able to patch up the hole in my heart pretty well. Hopefully, with more time, I’ll be able to truly open my heart again. Until then, I’m gonna focus on writing and pajama fighting.

Question: How do I live a good life of travels and tourism?
Old_Answer: I’ve been on 21 trips this year. It’s not all it’s cracked up to be. This photo is from Burano, Italy, where I spent a day a few weeks ago with my girlfriend. It’s a beautiful, small town just outside of Venice. We had to take a boat taxi to get there. How did I get to live a life of travel and (relatively frequent) tourism? Well, it was pretty simple. You can probably do it too. First, I was a brat who decided that he didn’t want to work “a real job”. When I was younger, I worked normal young person jobs, but there’s a gap on my resume from the time I was 22 onward. I worked in a restaurant when I was younger. I was a camp counselor. The reason? I became a “professional Jiu-Jitsu athlete” and “internet writer” instead. I gave up the stability to teach kids Jiu-Jitsu, private lessons (through word-of-mouth marketing alone), and create an online content portfolio. For a few years, my parents thought I was out of my f*cking mind. I lived in a shitty studio apartment where my rent was incredibly cheap — although, when I moved in, I couldn’t even afford it. A story for another day. On the side, I wrote copy for small businesses. I hustled like a maniac. My personal development routine bordered on insane. I woke up at 6am every day and either wrote or worked out. I wrote and trained Jiu-Jitsu all day long. I didn’t have any money, so I just threw myself into my crafts — writing, competing in Jiu-Jitsu, and teaching. It was stupid. I wouldn’t recommend anyone live like this. I was unstable because I was financially unstable. I did not socialize. I had no friends (except my friends from Jiu-Jitsu). I trained so hard that my body broke and I wrote so much that I had wrist injuries. When this happened, I kept working and training. I was determined to do “something” for myself. In the end (long story short), the hard work paid off, and I was gifted the opportunity to travel full-time for about 6 months. During this time, I had pretty much every experience you can imagine. I had my heart broken. I fell in love. I failed and spent thousands of dollars on investments that I still haven’t seen a dime of return from. I achieved some major goals, like placing in one of the biggest martial arts tournaments in Europe (despite going up in weight and being injured). I also had some really fun travel experiences, like spending a week in Italy with my girlfriend, walking the sunny beaches of San Diego, road-tripping across America and listening to one of my favorite novels, or crossing the border south and seeing Mexico for the first time. I’ve gotten to do the whole “travel the world” thing like my old hero, Anthony Bourdain, and I didn’t have to inherit a bunch of money, have rich parents, or even get a high-paying job. I nickeled and dimed my way all the way across the world, a handful of times. I traveled the world while being an online writer and competing in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu — a grappling art that you probably have never heard of. That’s pretty cool to me. But that’s not the end of the story, unfortunately. Or, fortunately, depending on how you look at it. When I was younger, I wanted my life to look just like the movies. I wanted to fall in love in Venice (I did), I wanted to work on my first book on a rainy day from a cafe in London, and I wanted to sip coffee with an eager grin while overlooking the Rocky Mountains. I wanted all these idyllic, movie-esque experiences, and I got them because I sought them. But they did not make me happy. They did not heal the wounds in my heart put there by past torments. Travel did not make me a happy person. You don’t need happiness or the novelty of travel to be complete, you need meaning. The problem is that a lot of us are so disconnected from meaning in our daily lives that the only place that we truly find it is through travel. When I was traveling the world, you know what I longed for? To be somewhere like where I am now, relaxing after a hard workout, writing something that interests me, and sipping a hot coffee while my beautiful girlfriend reads in the other room (she took this picture). Home is here. Travel is fun and can offer some fun experiences, but home is here.

Question: Should I learn judo or jiu jitsu?
Old_Answer: If you’re 6 and want to try and make it to the Olympics in 12 years, Judo. If you’re trying to learn how to actually fight someone, do Jiu-Jitsu. If you want to make money in martial arts, do Jiu-Jitsu. If you want to be a part of one of the fastest-growing martial arts in the world (behind probably only MMA), do Jiu-Jitsu. Judo focuses on throws and upper body attacks. In Judo, there’s also an aspect of the training called “newaza”, which translates to ground techniques. That’s basically Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. Essentially, Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu is newaza on steroids. This is because “newaza” is very limited. It ignores many aspects of grappling. I submitted a Judo Junior Olympian when I was just a purple belt in Jiu-Jitsu. He was quite upset about it. Leg locks are also illegal in judo. On the flipside, they are a centerpiece of learning modern Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. “Why would you ignore 50% of the human body?” is a cliche quote in BJJ at this point from BJJ legend Dean Lister (to John Danaher, who made the quote famous). Just about all Judo that I’m familiar with is done in the gi (I think there’s some no-gi Judo, it’s just uncommon). In Jiu-Jitsu, the average practitioner will practice both gi and no-gi every week. Modern Jiu-Jitsu is becoming a blend of Judo, freestyle and Greco Roman wrestling, Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, sambo, and even American catch wrestling. It’s becoming really cool to watch and participate in. The other thing I like about BJJ is that the culture is very modern. BJJ is always evolving and it’s evolving very quickly. There’s no “old school martial arts bullshit”. I’m an adult. I don’t need some dude who I call “sifu” or “sensei” who tells me what moves I’m allowed to do and what is off-limits. I don’t need anyone telling me who I can’t train with and learn from. I train with friends from other academies all the time. I fly all over the world to train with people. I watch moves on Instagram and try to learn them. That’s how technical evolution happens in the modern world. Plus, now, there are even professional Jiu-Jitsu events all over the place to study and learn from. This weekend, I’m competing in one in California for $5000. Not a horrible prize for an emerging professional sport. When I was a white belt in 2015, there were only a handful of professional Jiu-Jitsu promotions in the world. Now, there are dozens. Some events are paying up to $100,000 in cash prizes. I’ve never seen this in Judo. This actually goes back to the point I made in the opening sentence. In part because there is no BJJ in the Olympics, the sport of Jiu-Jitsu is exploding. BJJ is entirely private. The early days of BJJ were financed by rich dudes who just wanted to see the art grow. The Olympics or any other large government body isn’t holding back the development of the sport, so it’s growing like crazy. People in Jiu-Jitsu don’t care about bureaucratic bullshit. People in Jiu-Jitsu do Jiu-Jitsu to escape that shit. In wrestling and judo, it’s also really hard to make money. Owning a judo school typically isn’t a super profitable business (how many working professionals want to get thrown on their heads after work?), and private wrestling schools are few and far between. There is also no money available for professional athletes in these sports. A top-of-the-line Jiu-Jitsu academy on the other hand can make 6 figures (or even more). Jiu-Jitsu as a community has also strived to create a culture that is accessible and appealing to the average person. As a result of this exploding culture, you’re seeing more and more professional Jiu-Jitsu athletes. The level of the sport is rising year after year. This year’s ADCC World Championship (Abu Dhabi Combat Club) in Las Vegas is going to be insane. You, the person reading this, can head down to your local BJJ academy tomorrow and take your first introduction class. Depending on where you go, you can probably take it for free. Jiu-Jitsu people just want you to join the culture. If the culture grows, we all live easier, get better, and learn more. That’s what Jiu-Jitsu is really about and that’s why I like it more than any other martial art.

I could never do it. I could hardly walk more than a few steps. I was never a good hand-walker. I was also never a state champion. I was average in all things combat sports for the entirety of my youth. I didn’t win anything that mattered until I was 22. By that time, I had been involved in combat sports for more than a decade and I was doing it for the love of it. By the time I had any real success on the mat, I was already intrinsically motivated, and that gave me the work ethic to develop the skill required to have competitive success. As a side project, I still never gave up on my hand-walking, either. By the time I could walk to the end of the mat on my hands, I was already a Jiu-Jitsu world champion, and I was walking on my hands for the hell of it. I’ve realized that my wrestling lessons have helped me develop intrinsic motivation from a pretty young age, and as a coach, I try to help people do the same things. I realized this more as a coach than an athlete, but it is true in whatever you do: intrinsic motivation is the key to achieving difficult goals over extended periods of time. This is how you can teach people to develop intrinsic motivation. If you can do x, you can (maybe) do y. One thing that I hear a lot in the writing world is something along the lines of “if you write every day for 10 years, you will be a 6-figure writer”. Unfortunately, the way the market works, this is not necessarily true. You might not attain any success in writing. Nothing is guaranteed. If you write every day, that doesn’t mean that you will be the next Stephen King or Mark Manson. However, I can guarantee that if you don’t practice writing just about every day, you will definitely not achieve any success in writing. The same is true for music. The same is true for Jiu-Jitsu. In order to develop the ability to do the work required to do something incredibly well, you have to do the thing not because you want to be good, but because you love doing the thing. You must drop the results-driven approach, and seek “flow”. This is what I taught a 6-year-old how to do over the last few months. If a child can learn to flow, so can you. My work life is split about 50% between writing and teaching/competing in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. Most of my teaching income comes through private lessons and teaching classes at a local academy here in Chicago, where I teach kid’s Jiu-Jitsu classes 3 days per week. I’ve done this for 6 months now, and when I first started, I had the kids “walk on their hands” for one of their warm-up exercises. As a joke, I channeled my wrestling coach told them that if they could walk all the way down to the end of the mat on their hands without falling, they’d be world champions. When we started doing “handstand walks” during class, none of them could make it more than a few feet. Most of them still can’t. Most of them are not physically developed enough yet to walk on their hands. However, some of them love walking on their hands. For a few of my students, the difficult task of walking on your hands as far as you can is their favorite part of Jiu-Jitsu class. One kid who loves this a lot is Armani. “Coach, can we walk on our hands today?” Every single day that Armani is in class, he runs over to me during warm-ups and asks me if we can walk on our hands. Every. Single. Day. The only question I get asked more than “Coach, can we play dodgeball?” is “Coach, can we walk on our hands?”. Kids are funny like that. They’re consistent. Armani is undeniably consistent. When he started walking on his hands, he couldn’t get more than a few steps. After a few months of watching me walk on my hands, getting some pointers, and practicing at home on his own, Armani was able to walk almost all the way down the mat. That was when I decided to make a friendly competition out of our daily hand-walking exercise. “Whoever is the first person to walk all the way down the mat on their hands will get a candy bar of their choice from me,” I said one day a few weeks back. After I said this, a funny thing happened. Intrinsic motivation is the key to perfection. Once I presented the students with the option to win a candy bar, some of them started to practice hand-walking before and after class. They desperately wanted that free candy. Who wouldn't? To answer my own question — Armani wouldn’t. Armani didn’t. For Armani, this extrinsic motivation did very little for him because he was already intrinsically motivated. A few classes later, Armani successfully walked all the way down to the end of the mat on his hands without a problem. After he did this, I pulled him aside. “What kind of candy bar do you want? You won.” “What do you mean?” he replied. He had completely forgotten about the challenge. He was walking on his hands every day not because he wanted to win, not because he wanted a candy bar from Coach, but because he just liked walking on his hands. He won himself a free Milky Way bar that didn’t even really need. He earned it through hard work, dedication, and most importantly, enjoying the activity that he was doing. That last point is the most important. In closing… The most important aspect of learning to do difficult things is not being gritty, being tough, or even being resilient. The most important aspect of learning to develop a high level of skills over an extended period of time is learning to enjoy the difficult skill. This is why I’m very grateful that I started wrestling when I was just 12. Legendary wrestler Dan Gable once said, “once you’ve wrestled, everything else in life is easy”. Obviously, this isn’t really true, but there is some truth to it. Becoming a successful writer, grappler, business owner, or anything is still difficult when you have wrestling experience. However, what wrestling and other physical endeavors inadvertently teach you is to love the grind for the grind itself. There were moments during my career when I was completely miserable and the thought of dying was literally more appealing than stepping onto the mat. However, now, when I look back at my wrestling days, I can’t help but reminisce about the early morning bus rides in the freezing Chicago winter, the ridiculously hard workouts at all hours of the day, and the constant soreness and hunger that I felt when wrestling was my entire life. I sense that little Armani is going to feel a similar type of way about walking on his hands one day. He’s going to think it’s hard, he’s going think it’s frustrating, but he’s also going to think it’s an incredibly fun activity to do. Learning to love doing difficult things for no other reason than the fact that they’re fun is the key to doing difficult things easily.

Old_Answer: Traveling alone is hard. I did the math today, and I’ve been on 19 trips this year for Jiu-Jitsu competitions, seminars, and training trips. I’m in San Diego right now, for the third time since June. The city is starting to feel familiar. I can get around parts of it without using my maps app. This trip is a little different than the last time I was here though, because I’m traveling by myself. It’s cool to get in a new place and do my favorite thing—I’m here to train and film an instructional DVD for my Jiu-Jitsu—but it’s a little lonely when I’m not at the gym. Last week I was in Toledo, Ohio, for training. It was fun to train and I definitely got better, but I missed my friends. The other night, I drove home to Chicago, and then the next morning I hopped on a plane and flew out here to SD. Loneliness in the road can be difficult to tame. I chose this life, I’m just a little lonely sometimes lately. Part of me longs for somewhere that feels like home. I’ve been on the road so much this year I don’t really remember what home feels like. One tip that’s helped me mentally when I travel alone has been learning to address my emotional needs by myself. If I’m lonely, I find someone to talk to. This is essential for me. If there’s no one to talk to (the 2 people I’m friends with in San Diego were busy today), I find some work to distract myself. I’ve been working a lot lately—-writing, training, teaching, etc. I’m not posting as many original Quora answers lately in part because I’m kind of sick of getting yelled at by people every time I open this app, but also because I’m focusing a bit more on the writing that is going to help me grow my career a bit. I’m trying to next the step, and I feel I’m getting closer. That’s why I keep traveling. I’m focusing on the mission. The mission requires travel, even when the beauty of travel is gone.
